GUIDE 01

What counts as "5-axis" printing?

A printer earns the label when the nozzle and the part can be re-oriented relative to each other while printing — three linear axes (X, Y, Z) plus two rotary axes working together. The rotary axes can live in three places: in the table (a tilting, rotating trunnion), in the head (a swivelling nozzle), or split between both. Each choice changes the machine's stiffness, collision behaviour and usable volume.

Two distinctions matter more than the axis count:

  • 3+2 (indexed) — re-orient between sections, print flat layers within each. Easier, but the layers stay flat and seams appear.
  • Simultaneous 5-axis — all axes interpolate during deposition, orientation changes continuously, and layers can genuinely curve. This is the mode conformal printing needs.
  • RTCP is not optional. Without rotation tool-centre-point compensation, tilting the machine drags the nozzle off its programmed path. Any serious 5-axis claim should name how the controller handles it.
GUIDE 02

Non-planar slicing, explained

A conventional slicer intersects the model with horizontal planes and emits flat perimeters. A non-planar slicer instead generates toolpaths on the part's surfaces: offsetting paths across the geometry, assigning each point a nozzle orientation (usually the surface normal), then checking the whole motion for collisions between nozzle, part and machine.

  • Orientation is a field, not a setting — it varies continuously across the part and drives both rotary axes at every moment.
  • Extrusion must adapt — layer thickness and flow change where surfaces tilt and converge; flat-slicer flow maths doesn't carry over.
  • The output is still G-code — but with A/B (rotary) words on most moves, which is why ordinary printer firmware can't run it.
  • Support logic inverts — instead of propping up overhangs, the slicer re-orients the part so overhangs become printable walls.

This is why the software, not the frame, is the field's bottleneck — and why slicer collaboration is half of what we do.

GUIDE 03

Reading the landscape: six routes to multi-axis

"Multi-axis printing" covers machines with very different ambitions. Trunnion-table FDM (our route) targets true conformal layers at bench scale. Tilting-head designs keep a big flat bed but fight head collisions. 3+2 indexing is the pragmatic middle. Belt printers add one endless axis for long parts at a fixed angle — useful, but not conformal. Robotic arms trade accuracy for metre-scale freedom. Print-and-mill hybrids buy surface finish with a machining pass, at hybrid prices.

The full comparison — strengths, limits, maturity, and named projects for each route — is in the technology landscape below. If a route or project is missing, that is a bug in this page, and the contribution path is how it gets fixed.

GUIDE 04

Starting 5-axis research: a practical checklist

For labs setting up a non-planar programme, the questions that save the most time are asked before any hardware arrives:

  • Fix your benchmark geometries first — a dome (stair-stepping), a 70° overhang wall (support-free claim), a curved duct (internal access), a print onto a curved substrate. Every route can be compared on the same four parts.
  • Decide what you will measure — surface roughness on curves, interlayer strength along vs. across conformal layers, dimensional error vs. tilt angle. Publishable claims need these numbers.
  • Budget for the slicer, not just the machine — seats, development time or a collaboration agreement; hardware without toolpaths is furniture.
  • Plan to publish the failures — collision cases, singularity behaviour, failed orientations. In a field this young, negative results are the scarcest resource.
Why conformal

Flat layers are the compromise. Curved layers are the point.

A 3-axis printer can only stack horizontal slices, so every curved surface becomes a staircase and every overhang needs scaffolding. Add rotary axes and keep the nozzle normal to the surface, and the geometry rules change completely.

01

Overhangs & undercuts, support-free

By tilting the part as it grows, walls and undercuts that would need support structures on a flat-layer machine print self-supported. No supports to design, print, break off and sand away — and internal, curved geometries that flat slicing simply cannot reach become printable.

02

Strength along the surface

FDM parts are weakest across layer lines. Conformal layers run along the part's surface — along the load path — instead of slicing across it, so curved shells, ducts and brackets behave more like the continuous material they imitate.

03

Smooth curves, no stair-stepping

Layers that follow the surface eliminate the staircase finish on domes, tubes and freeform shells — the surfaces come off the machine smooth, with far less post-processing, which matters for airflow, fluid flow and anything that touches skin.

04

Print onto existing parts

Five axes let you deposit onto curved, already-existing objects: add features to a printed or machined substrate, repair a worn curved surface, or print directly onto a shell. The substrate becomes part of the build — a research direction flat-layer machines can't explore at all.

Control & software

The hard part isn't the frame. It's six axes moving as one, and a slicer that thinks in surfaces.

Five-axis printing fails or succeeds in the control stack. Ours pairs a multi-axis controller with RTCP — the tool centre point stays exactly on the programmed path while the machine re-orients around it — with our own curved-surface slicing software, developed alongside the hardware since 2022.

Real multi-axis control, with RTCP

Six axes — X, Y, Z plus the A, B and C rotary axes — interpolate simultaneously under the POCENDER / PCD3D controller, with RTCP (rotation tool centre point) keeping the nozzle tip exactly on the programmed path while the machine re-orients around it. Without RTCP, tilting the part drags the nozzle off its path; with it, conformal toolpaths stay true.

  • Simultaneous interpolation across linear and rotary axes
  • Touchscreen control on the machine
  • Per-axis travel, speed and acceleration parameters

A slicer that thinks in surfaces — and remote operation

Our slicing software generates toolpaths on the part's surfaces instead of in flat planes — the software half of conformal printing, and an active research topic in its own right. The machine itself runs from a touchscreen or remotely through the POCENDER web panel: jog every axis, manage files, update firmware and monitor status from a phone or laptop. On custom builds, the stack extends further:

  • AI-assisted simulation of the print before it runs
  • In-process self-inspection with automatic compensation
  • Full remote control for shared and teaching labs

Technology landscape

Every serious route to printing in more than three axes, on one map.

A field becomes navigable when its options are named and compared honestly. This map is maintained as a public reference: routes, trade-offs, maturity — and the projects pursuing each route. It is deliberately incomplete, and it improves through contributions.

Tilt–rotate table (trunnion) FDM

Route 1 · True conformal

The part rides a table that tilts and rotates beneath a conventional 3-axis gantry, so the surface being printed is always presented to the nozzle at the right angle. Strengths: stiff, compact, genuinely simultaneous 5-axis motion; the extruder stays upright, so filament feeding behaves normally.

Limits: the usable volume shrinks as the table tilts; tall parts swing through a large envelope; collision checking between part, table and gantry is mandatory.

● Our platform's route Research + early builds

Tilting / swivelling print head

Route 2 · True conformal

The rotary axes live in a wrist at the nozzle, which leans to stay normal to the surface while the part sits still. Strengths: works over a full-size flat bed; large parts don't move; natural fit for printing onto big stationary substrates.

Limits: the head itself becomes the collision problem — hotend, fans and cabling sweep a wide cone; extruders fed at steep angles behave badly; wrist stiffness limits speed and quality.

Research

3+2 indexed printing

Route 3 · Indexed

Re-orient the part between sections; print each section with ordinary flat layers. Strengths: by far the simplest control and slicing of any multi-axis route; reaches faces a 3-axis machine can't; reduces supports substantially.

Limits: layers are still flat within each section, so stair-stepping remains; seams and registration errors appear where orientations meet; not conformal printing, despite frequent marketing to the contrary.

Research · niche tools

Belt & continuous-axis printing

Route 4 · One extra axis

A conveyor-belt bed (or a continuously rotating fixture) prints at a fixed 45°-style angle, giving an effectively infinite axis for very long parts and natural support-free overhangs in one direction. Strengths: commercially available, affordable, excellent for long profiles and batch production of identical parts.

Limits: a single fixed orientation — no second rotary axis, no surface-following layers. An adjacent technology to 5-axis printing, not a subset of it.

Commercial niche

Robotic-arm extrusion

Route 5 · Large scale

An industrial robot arm (six or more degrees of freedom) carries an extruder, often pellet-fed, over metre-scale parts. Strengths: unmatched reach and orientation freedom; prints furniture-, boat- and building-scale geometry; non-planar toolpaths at architectural scale.

Limits: arm stiffness and path accuracy are far below gantry machines; cost, cell footprint and safety requirements exclude most labs; fine conformal detail is not its game.

Early commercial · large format

5-axis hybrid: print + CNC mill

Route 6 · Hybrid

One machine deposits material with multi-axis motion, then machines it to tolerance in the same setup. Strengths: the only route that pairs conformal geometry with machined surface finish and accuracy; powerful for tooling and end-use metal-adjacent workflows.

Limits: highest cost and complexity on this map; two process disciplines to master; mostly aimed at industrial users rather than research exploration.

Early commercial · industrial

Projects & players worth knowing

A snapshot of the field as of November 2026, across academia, open source and industry. Inclusion is informational, not endorsement — and the list is openly incomplete. Missing someone? Tell us.

Open5xImperial College London · open source

An open-source tilt–rotate hardware add-on that converts a conventional desktop printer into a 5-axis machine, with non-planar slicing built on Rhino/Grasshopper. The reference point for the DIY-and-research end of Route 1, and proof that the retrofit path is real — controller and slicer included.

5AxisMakerLondon · desktop hybrid

One of the earliest desktop machines to combine 5-axis CNC milling and 3D printing in a single unit — an early commercial attempt at Route 6, years before "hybrid" became a category.

Ai BuildLondon · robotic cells

Large-format robotic printing cells and the software to drive them — a leading name on Route 5, focused on industrial and architectural-scale parts.

Branch TechnologyUSA · construction scale

Robotic "cellular fabrication": freeform lattice structures printed with arms and assembled into architectural walls — Route 5 pushed to building scale.

Blackbelt & Creality CR-30Belt printing · commercial

The machines that made Route 4 real products: conveyor-bed printers for infinite-length parts, widely used for batch profiles — and the most common source of "isn't that 5-axis?" confusion this page exists to clear up.

University research groupsWorldwide · slicing & motion

Much of the field's slicing theory — orientation fields, collision-free non-planar path generation, multi-axis process planning — comes from university groups publishing papers and prototypes rather than products. Our own slicer work with institute and university partners since 2022 sits in this tradition.

Glossary

The words of the field, defined once and used consistently.

Multi-axis printing borrows vocabulary from CNC machining, slicing software and printed electronics — and the same word doesn't always mean the same thing in each. These are the definitions this site uses.

5-axis 3D printing
Additive manufacturing where the nozzle and part re-orient relative to each other during printing — three linear axes plus two rotary axes — so material can be deposited along directions other than straight up.
Conformal printing
Layers that follow (conform to) a curved surface — the surface of the growing part, or an existing object. In printed electronics the word centres on printing onto existing surfaces; in FDM it usually means curved layers. This site uses it for both, and says which.
Non-planar printing
Toolpaths not confined to flat horizontal planes, producing curved layers. Used almost interchangeably with "conformal" in the FDM community; the stricter term of the two.
RTCPROTATION TOOL CENTRE POINT
Controller compensation that keeps the nozzle tip exactly on the programmed toolpath while rotary axes move. Without it, every tilt displaces the tip and conformal paths distort — the single best question to ask any "5-axis" machine.
Trunnion
A tilting-and-rotating work table carrying the part through both rotary axes, inherited from 5-axis CNC machining. The most common configuration in desktop 5-axis printing — including our platform.
3+2 printingINDEXED
Re-orient between sections, print flat layers within each. Simpler in every way than simultaneous motion — and not conformal, whatever the brochure says.
Simultaneous interpolation
All axes moving together under one coordinated motion command, so orientation changes continuously while material is deposited. The motion mode true curved layers require.
Stair-stepping
The stepped finish flat layers leave on any curved surface. Thinner layers shrink the steps but never remove them; curved layers eliminate the cause rather than the symptom.
Substrate printing
Printing onto an existing object — printed, machined or moulded — instead of a flat bed, following its surface with multi-axis orientation. Enables repair, added features and personalisation.
Self-supporting angle
The steepest overhang a process can print without support. On a 3-axis machine it's roughly 45° from vertical; a 5-axis machine changes the angle itself by re-orienting the part, which is the whole trick.
Orientation field
The assignment of a nozzle direction to every point of a non-planar toolpath — the core data a conformal slicer computes, and the thing flat slicers don't have at all.
Singularity
A pose where a rotary axis must spin infinitely fast to maintain the path — a real failure mode of 5-axis toolpaths near vertical orientations, handled (or not) by the slicer and controller.
Who it's for

An exploration, open to the people equipped to explore it.

Conformal printing is not a settled technology — the slicing theory, the motion strategies and the applications are all still being worked out, in public, by a small worldwide community. This platform exists for the people doing that work.

R1

Research institutes & university labs

Groups working on non-planar slicing, multi-axis motion, materials behaviour on curved layers, or conformal applications — who need real five-axis hardware to run experiments on, not just simulations. Joint development and slicer collaboration are how we've worked with institutes and universities since 2022.

R2

Teaching labs

Five-axis machining is standard curriculum; five-axis printing is not — yet. A benchtop machine with an open control stack gives students genuine multi-axis, RTCP and non-planar toolpath concepts on hardware they can see, measure and modify.

R3

Advanced makers & small studios

Experienced builders who have hit the wall of flat-layer printing — support scars on every curve, weak shells, impossible undercuts — and want to experiment with the technology the community itself voted the next core direction of FDM.

R4

Application pioneers

Teams exploring where conformal printing wins first: printing onto existing objects, curved functional surfaces, wearables and prosthetics, aerodynamic and fluid shells. If your application needs a machine variant that doesn't exist yet, that's a custom-build conversation.

Where we honestly are

This is a prototype platform, not a production product. Machines are built one at a time, to order, and the design is still evolving — you will find rough edges, and current builds are not yet at production-level repeatability or polish. We don't publish a catalogue price, a fixed lead time or fleet-support promises, because at this stage those numbers wouldn't be honest.

What you get instead: direct access to the engineers, a machine configured for your questions, and a say in where the platform goes next. The labs and makers who join at this stage are the ones shaping what five-axis conformal printing becomes.

Open research agenda

The open research agenda: what this field still has to solve.

Not a list of solved applications — the standing problem list for conformal printing, with the status of each item as we currently see it. Statuses are reviewed as work in the field progresses; if your group has moved one of these, send the evidence and the agenda gets updated.

Q1 Conformal electronics & antennas

Traces, antennas and sensor patterns belong on curved surfaces, not flat boards folded to fit. Printing structure — and eventually conductive paths — directly onto curved shells is one of the most-cited reasons labs want true non-planar toolpaths.

Agenda · awaits conductive-path maturity

Q2 Printing onto existing objects

Scan a curved substrate, register the toolpath to it, and add material exactly where it's needed: features on printed or machined parts, repair of worn curved surfaces, personalisation of existing products. Flat-bed machines cannot do this at all.

Active on our platform

Q3 Curved composite shells

Shells, ducts and housings whose strength comes from fibre laid along the curve. Conformal layers put continuous material along the load path instead of chopping it into flat slices — a measurable mechanical question waiting for more data.

Open problem · comparative data wanted

Q4 Wearables, prosthetics & orthotics

Parts shaped by a body are curved in every direction. Support-free conformal printing promises smooth skin-contact surfaces and shells that follow anatomy without a staircase finish — a natural fit for research with clinical and design partners.

Exploring · partners welcome

Q5 Aerodynamic & fluid surfaces

Impellers, ducts, propellers and flow channels where surface quality is performance. Smooth curved layers remove the stair-stepping that disturbs flow, and support-free printing opens internal channel geometries that flat slicing can't build.

Active on our platform

Q6 The slicing problem itself

Generating collision-free, well-oriented non-planar toolpaths on arbitrary geometry is an open algorithmic problem. Our slicer is a working answer, developed with academic partners — and collaboration on it is one of the fastest ways to move the whole field.

Our core collaboration topic

FAQ

Straight answers, including the uncomfortable ones.

What is conformal (non-planar) 5-axis 3D printing?+

A conventional FDM printer stacks flat layers and can only move in X, Y and Z. A 5-axis machine adds rotary axes, so the nozzle stays normal to the surface being printed and the layers themselves curve to follow the part — that is conformal, or non-planar, printing. Overhangs and undercuts print without support structures, curved shells come out smooth instead of stair-stepped, and material is laid along the surface, where the loads run, instead of across flat slices.

Is this a production-ready machine I can buy off the shelf?+

Not yet — and we would rather say so plainly. The platform is at prototype stage: every machine is built to order, configured with the buyer, and still evolving. It is not a mass-produced, lights-out production printer, and it rewards users who are technically engaged. If you need certified fleet repeatability today, this is not the right purchase yet. If you want to research, teach or push non-planar printing — and shape the machine while you do — this is exactly the stage to join.

Who is the machine for?+

Research institutes and university labs working on non-planar printing, multi-axis motion or slicing algorithms; teaching labs that want students on real five-axis hardware; and advanced makers and small studios who have hit the limits of flat-layer printing. Typical projects include conformal printing research, curved composite shells, printing onto existing curved parts, and custom machine or slicer development with us.

How large a part can it print?+

The current reference prototype is configured with axis travel of X 220 × Y 190 × Z 180 mm. The usable conformal volume is smaller than the travel box and depends on part geometry and tilt angles — send us your model and we will check it honestly. Custom builds can be specified with different travels.

Which materials does it print?+

It is an FDM (FFF) platform, and the hotend and thermal configuration are set per build. Common requests are PLA, PETG, ABS/ASA, TPU and fibre-filled filaments; if your project needs a specific engineering material, tell us in your first message and we will confirm whether and how the machine should be configured for it.

Can we collaborate on the slicing software or a custom machine?+

Yes — that is a core part of what we do. Since 2022 we have worked with research institutes and universities on multi-axis linkage control, curved-surface slicing software and customised machines, and a custom five-axis unit has already been built and delivered to a university research lab. Joint development, slicer collaboration and one-off custom builds are all conversations we welcome.

Do you ship internationally, and what does a machine cost?+

Yes, machines are built to order in Suzhou, China and can be shipped internationally in protective crating, with setup support by video call. There is no list price: configuration — travels, hotend, sensors, software options — changes every build, so each machine is quoted individually after we understand your project. Tell us what you want to print or research and we will reply with a configuration proposal and a price.

What is the difference between 3+2 and simultaneous 5-axis printing?+

In 3+2 (indexed) printing, the part is tilted to a new fixed orientation, then printed with ordinary flat layers before being re-oriented again — the rotary axes move between sections, not during them. In simultaneous 5-axis printing, all axes interpolate together while material is deposited, so the nozzle orientation changes continuously and the layers themselves curve. 3+2 is much simpler to control and slice, and it helps with access and support reduction, but only simultaneous motion produces true conformal layers and smooth curved surfaces.

Can a normal slicer like Cura or PrusaSlicer generate 5-axis toolpaths?+

No. Mainstream slicers assume flat, horizontal layers and three-axis motion; their output contains no rotary-axis moves and no toolpaths that follow a surface. Non-planar toolpaths require surface-based slicing — generating paths on the part's geometry, checking nozzle orientation and collisions in five axes — which is why dedicated curved-surface slicers, including ours and research tools such as the Open5x Grasshopper workflow, exist. This software gap, more than hardware, is what keeps 5-axis printing a research field today.

5-axis printer, robotic arm or belt printer — which route should I choose?+

They solve different problems. A 5-axis FDM machine (tilt-rotate table or tilting head) is the route to true conformal layers on desktop-scale parts — the right choice for non-planar research. A robotic arm trades stiffness and accuracy for scale and freedom, and suits large-format work. A belt printer adds one continuous axis for very long parts printed at a fixed angle, but cannot re-orient in two rotary axes, so it is not conformal printing. Our technology landscape compares the routes in detail.

Can I retrofit a normal 3-axis printer into a 5-axis machine?+

As a research project, yes — the open-source Open5x project, for example, adds a tilt-rotate stage to a conventional printer. But the mechanics are the easy half: you also need a controller that interpolates five axes with tool-centre compensation (RTCP), and a slicer that can generate non-planar toolpaths at all. Most groups who price the full stack — mechanics, controller, software, calibration time — find a purpose-built platform the shorter path, which is why both routes appear in our landscape map.

I found an error, or a project missing from the landscape — can I contribute?+

Please do. This site is maintained as a reference for the whole field, not just as our product page. Use the contact form below, choose “Contribute to the hub”, and send the correction, paper, project or resource — with a link. Substantive contributions are credited on the page.
